meta.title: Casalia · Spanish house price forecasts
meta.description: 12-month forecasts of the appraised price per m² in every Spanish region, backtested over 16 years and published before the outcome is known.

hero.answer: Where the appraised price per m² is heading in every Spanish region, from official data. Every year from 2010 to 2025 was forecast by models trained only on earlier years.
hero.description: Ridge regression, gradient boosting and a PyTorch network compete against simple rules over the same test years. So far momentum, a rule that repeats the last 12 months' change, has done best, so it provides the main forecast, with an 80% range. Gradient boosting runs alongside, explained with SHAP. Each quarter's forecasts are committed before the outcome is known.

graphic.modelsSub: Simple rules vs Ridge, gradient boosting, PyTorch MLP
graphic.outputSub: ML forecast + SHAP · logged in advance

forecasts.title: Forecasts
forecasts.subtitle: Forecast change in the average appraised price per m² between {{origin}} and {{target}}, by region. Published on {{generated}}.
forecasts.error: The forecasts could not be loaded.
forecasts.championNote: Momentum carries the last 12 months' change forward. It had the lowest error in both backtest periods, so it leads.
forecasts.intervalNote: The range comes from momentum's own past errors. It covered 78% of outcomes in 2010-2021 and 76% in 2022-2025, though only 42-50% in its worst years. Most of it lies above the forecast because momentum has underestimated the recent rise.
forecasts.homeNote: This is the regional change applied to your figure, not a valuation of your home.
forecasts.smallMarket: Small market: few appraisals per quarter, so the data are noisy.
forecasts.challengerNote: It runs in shadow mode, logged and scored next to the main forecast. It would take over only if it beat momentum by more than the margin of error.
forecasts.shapNote: SHAP shows how much each group of inputs moved this forecast away from the model's average. It explains the model, not the market.
forecasts.gapBelow: The ML forecast is below the main one in {{below}} of {{total}} regions, and outside the main forecast's 80% range in {{outside}}. The ML model expects prices to grow more slowly than over the last 12 months.
forecasts.gapAbove: The ML forecast is above the main one in {{above}} of {{total}} regions, and outside the main forecast's 80% range in {{outside}}. The ML model expects prices to grow faster than over the last 12 months.
forecasts.gapHistory: It made the same kind of call in 2022-2025, and in each of those years prices rose more than it expected. The forecast log will show who is right this time.
forecasts.rowLabel: {{name}}: main forecast {{main}}, 80% range {{low}} to {{high}}, ML forecast {{ml}}
forecasts.log: These forecasts were committed to the repository before the outcome was known and will be scored when MIVAU publishes the {{target}} data.

results.title: Out-of-sample results
results.intro: Mean absolute error (MAE) of the 12-month change, in percentage points (pp); lower is better. Models are retrained every year, and each forecast only uses data up to the quarter it starts from.
results.devSub: 792 forecasts per model, used to choose models and settings
results.holdoutSub: 238 forecasts per model, fixed in a commit before scoring
results.devNote: Gradient boosting was 0.31 pp worse than momentum on average and better in 4 of 12 years; the gap is within the margin of error (95% block-bootstrap interval: −0.29 to +0.91 pp).
results.holdoutNote: Momentum was best in all four years, a period of shocks the models had never seen. In 2022 inflation ran at 5.7-12.1%, above anything in training. In 2022-23 the Euribor rose by up to 3.9 pp in a year; the largest earlier rise in the data was 1.4 pp.
results.mlpNote: The MLP is the PyTorch network from the first version of the project. With about 400 to 1,500 training rows per fold, simpler models did better.
results.diagIntro: Before the analysis, I committed a plan: two hypotheses and how to test them. Then I ran grouped SHAP and refitted the model leaving out one group of inputs at a time. As the plan notes, the inflation hypothesis came from an earlier look at 2022.

diag.2022: Inflation ran at 5.7-12.1%, beyond anything in training (the maximum was 5.6%, in 2008). Trees can't extrapolate, so the model treated 2022 like 2008 and predicted falls while prices rose.
diag.2023: The jump in the Euribor pulled the forecasts down.
diag.2024: Partly rates again. Not covered by either hypothesis: refitting without the momentum inputs cut that year's error by 4.2 pp.
diag.2025: Neither hypothesis holds, so that year is still unexplained.

data.title: Official data
data.desc: Appraised price per m² (MIVAU); CPI, mortgages and unemployment (INE); and the 12-month Euribor (ECB). Prices go back to 1995, but the model data start in 2004, when every source is available, and cover 17 regions plus Ceuta and Melilla. One script rebuilds the dataset from the sources.

leakage.title: No look-ahead
leakage.desc: Features use only data up to the quarter the forecast starts from. A training example is used only once its outcome has been observed, and no forecast is made until every source has published that quarter's data.

walkforward.title: Walk-forward evaluation
walkforward.desc: Each year is forecast by models trained and tuned only on earlier years. The last four years were frozen in a commit before being scored, and haven't changed since.

baselines.title: Baselines first
baselines.desc: Ridge regression, gradient boosting and a PyTorch MLP are compared with three simple rules: no change, momentum and the historical mean. Momentum had the lowest error in both periods, so it leads. Another model replaces it only if it wins by more than the margin of error (a confidence interval that excludes zero).

uncertainty.title: Measured uncertainty
uncertainty.desc: The 80% range comes from momentum's own errors over the last five years. The repository reports, year by year, how often the outcome fell inside it, including the years it fell short of 80%.

explain.title: Explained and logged
explain.desc: The ML model is explained with grouped TreeSHAP. Each quarter's forecasts are committed before the outcome is known, so they can't be edited after the fact.

limits.appraisal: Appraised prices move more smoothly than sale prices, which is part of why momentum does well.
limits.revised: The data are today's revised series, not what was known at the time, so the backtest is pseudo out-of-sample.
limits.turns: Momentum and its range do worst when the market changes direction or pace, as in 2012-14, 2019-20 and 2024.
limits.small: Ceuta and Melilla are tiny markets and are shown separately.

footer.story: Casalia started in 2026 as my final project for a vocational diploma in software development (DAM): a PyTorch network and this web app. I later rebuilt it from scratch on official data, with a proper walk-forward backtest. Now every forecast is published before its outcome is known.
